blocks.content:
The **multiplicity** of a zero $a$ of $P(x)$ is the number of times $(x-a)$ occurs as a factor of $P(x)$. A repeated zero has multiplicity greater than 1.

If $P(x)=(x-a)^mQ(x)$, where $Q(a)\ne0$, then $x=a$ is a zero of multiplicity $m$ of $P(x)$.

Multiplicity of zeroes tells us the behaviour of the curve at the $x$-intercepts.

content.prompt: Consider the polynomial equation $x^4-6x^3+11x^2-4x-4=0$. Show that $x=2$ is a double root of the equation. Hence solve the equation.

answer.worked:
Let $P(x)=x^4-6x^3+11x^2-4x-4$.
$$\begin{align*}P(2)&=16-48+44-8-4=0\\P'(x)&=4x^3-18x^2+22x-4\\P'(2)&=32-72+44-4=0\\P''(x)&=12x^2-36x+22\\P''(2)&=48-72+22=-2\ne0\end{align*}$$
Therefore $x=2$ has multiplicity exactly $2$. Let the remaining roots be $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Using the sum and product of the four roots:
$$\begin{align*}2+2+\alpha+\beta&=6\\\alpha+\beta&=2\\2\times2\times\alpha\beta&=-4\\\alpha\beta&=-1\end{align*}$$
The remaining roots satisfy
$$\begin{align*}x^2-2x-1&=0\\x&=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{4+4}}2\\x&=1\pm\sqrt2.\end{align*}$$
Thus $x=2$ (double root), $1+\sqrt2$ or $1-\sqrt2$.

content.prompt:
A polynomial is defined as $P(x) = (x - a)(x - b)^3(x - c)^2$.
If $ab > 0$ and $bc < 0$, which of the following could be the graph of $P(x)$?

$P(x)$ has degree $6$ and positive leading coefficient, so both ends of the graph rise.

The factor $(x-b)^3$ has multiplicity $3$, so the graph crosses the axis at $x=b$ with a horizontal tangent.

children.prompt: Prove that if $\alpha$ is a root of multiplicity $r$, where $r>1$, of a polynomial equation $P(x)=0$, then $\alpha$ is also a root of multiplicity $r-1$ of $P'(x)=0$.

answer.short: $P'(x)=(x-\alpha)^{r-1}[rQ(x)+(x-\alpha)Q'(x)]$, where $Q(\alpha)\ne0$. The bracket at $\alpha$ is $rQ(\alpha)\ne0$, so the multiplicity is exactly $r-1$.
answer.worked:
If $\alpha$ is a root of multiplicity $r$ of $P(x)=0$, then:
$$\begin{align*}
P(x) &= (x-\alpha)^rQ(x)
\end{align*}$$
where $Q(\alpha) \neq 0$.
Differentiating:
$$\begin{align*}
P'(x) &= r(x-\alpha)^{r-1}Q(x) + (x-\alpha)^rQ'(x) \\
&= (x-\alpha)^{r-1}\left[rQ(x) + (x-\alpha)Q'(x)\right]
\end{align*}$$
At $x=\alpha$:
$$\begin{align*}
rQ(\alpha) + (\alpha-\alpha)Q'(\alpha) &= rQ(\alpha) \\
&\neq 0
\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $\alpha$ is a root of multiplicity $r-1$ of $P'(x)=0$.

P(x) &= x^4 - 6x^2 - 8x - 3
\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}
P'(x) &= 4x^3 - 12x - 8 \\
P''(x) &= 12x^2 - 12
\end{align*}$$
Set $P''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{align*}
12x^2 - 12 &= 0 \\
x^2 &= 1 \\
x &= \pm 1
\end{align*}$$
Test $x=1$:
$$\begin{align*}
P'(1) &= 4 - 12 - 8 \\
&= -16
\end{align*}$$

Test $x=-1$:
$$\begin{align*}
P'(-1) &= -4 + 12 - 8 \\
&= 0 \\
P(-1) &= 1 - 6 + 8 - 3 \\
&= 0
\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $x=-1$ is the triple root.
$$\begin{align*}
P(x) &= (x+1)^3(x-3)
\end{align*}$$
Hence the roots are $x=-1$ with multiplicity $3$, and $x=3$.

answer.short: $p'(x)$ has no real zeroes, so $p$ is strictly monotonic and cuts the $x$-axis exactly once.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}p'(x)&=3ax^2+2bx+c\\\Delta&=(2b)^2-4(3a)(c)\\&=4(b^2-3ac)\end{aligned}$$
If $b^2-3ac<0$ then $\Delta<0$, so $p'(x)=0$ has no real roots. Hence $p'(x)$ has the same nonzero sign as $3a$ for all real $x$, and $p$ is strictly monotonic (always increasing or always decreasing).

Since $a\ne0$, $p$ is a continuous cubic whose values take opposite signs as $x\to\infty$ and $x\to-\infty$, so it cuts the $x$-axis at least once. Being strictly monotonic, it cannot cut it more than once. Hence $p(x)$ cuts the $x$-axis exactly once.

$$\begin{aligned}p''(x)&=6ax+2b\\p''\left(-\frac{b}{3a}\right)&=-2b+2b\\&=0\\p'''(x)&=6a\ne0\end{aligned}$$
So $p$, $p'$ and $p''$ all vanish at $x=-\dfrac{b}{3a}$ but $p'''$ does not. Hence the root has multiplicity exactly $3$.
